Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Muscle calcium stress cleaves junctophilin1, unleashing a gene regulatory program predicted to correct glucose dysregulation" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Richard Aldrich as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Enrique Jaimovich (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) The part of the paper including muscle biopsies from the MHS and MHN individuals appears unfinished. The authors need to include more MHN biopsies to be able to make any valuable comparisons, and for being able to conclude if there are any differences between MHS and MHN (and for respect to the individual donating muscle biopsies). One possibility is to submit the data later.

2) At present in the absence of a solid validation of the ability of antibodies A and B to recognize different band in western blot and in IMF experiments it is difficult to provide a positive answer to the present draft. Also the IMF images need to be carefully revised to provide clear support to the final conclusions.

3). Tammineni and co-authors provide a new interesting role in skeletal muscle for Junctophilin (44 kD segment, JPh44), where it translocates to the nuclei and interferes/affects transcription. Also, the authors shown that Calpain 1 can digest junctophilin to generate the 44 kDa segment. In general, the muscle field know little about how E-C coupling proteins have duals role and interfere/affect gene regulation that subsequently may alter the muscle function and metabolism. This part of the manuscript is solid, informative, and novel. In this paper, the authors also aim to link elevated Jph44 levels in muscle biopsies (myotubes) of patients with malignant hyperthermia susceptible (MHS) (that also exhibit elevated cytosolic calcium with calpain1-associated increases in Jph44 levels) to hyperglycemia in these patients via enhanced GSK3b activity (which inhibits glycogen synthase etc). This part of the manuscript is more speculative and descriptive and lacks proof-of-concept. Also, the authors often compare myotubes of "patients" (unclear whether this always is MHS, or MHN and MHS, needs to be specified) with murine myofibers (and these are presumably healthy controls, but needs to be clarified), and C2C12 myotubes (also control setting). These three vastly different muscle cells from both control and MH individuals makes any type of comparisons problematic and difficult to interpret the results and diverts ones focus from the more direct results regarding Caplain1- Jph44 – translocation – transcriptional changes. There is also data comparisons between myofibers and myotubes from control settings and how they link to MHS/MHN is difficult to interpret. The authors appear to still have access to MHS and MHN (control) samples, and thus to make the conclusions as suggested in the paper the authors need to include both MHS and MHN in all comparisons performed in the study.

Page 2, line 30-31: "On the other hand, LS Song and colleagues (27,30) provided evidence that the intra-nuclear actions of JPh2 31 fragments are "stress-adaptive", partially offsetting the negative consequences of activation of proteolysis". "Stress" can refer to many things, please define stress in this context.

4) Figure 1F, in comparison to other blots, it is not listed in the blot which protein was blotted for.

5) The authors name the JPh antibodies A and B, and then leave it for the reader to find information later in the text about them and how they differ, with the epitope binging to different part of the protein. Would be more reader friendly and informative to earlier in the text give information about the antibodies.

6). In the text the authors describe results as "highly significant" and "marginally significant", please define what p-values it refers to, respectively.

7) Page 4, line 14-16: "The tentative conclusion from this observation is that the cleavage process, which may operate in multiple sites and sequentially on cleaved products, blurs any detailed correspondence between increase in content of a given fragment and disappearance of the full-size protein". Please describe possible fragments that can be generated.

8_ The authors argue that a possible mechanism for that MHS patients develop hyperglycemia and thus at a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes, is that GSKb3 inhibits glycogen synthase. In this patient cohort (MHS, MHN), what was the fasting glucose levels? Moreover, skeletal muscle is efficient in taking up (e.g., GLUT4) storing (e.g., GS) and utilizing glucose and carbohydrates (glycolysis, TCA) whereas other tissues are lacking this capacity. Hence, how much difference in GSKb3 activity is needed to impact blood glucose levels on a systemic level? Also, what was the activity (phosphorylation) level of GSKb3 in the human samples? On the same note, the authors have previously reported a decrease in GLUT4 content in muscle from MHS individuals. The manuscript would benefit from that the authors acknowledged this finding and thus give a broader understanding of the alterations in glucose homeostasis that is observed in these individuals.

9) his might be a misunderstanding on my side, but I read it as the author hypothesize that elevated [ca2+]cyt ◊ Caplain 1 ◊ cleveage of JpH -> larger segments stays in cytosol but the Jph44 translocate to nuclei and impact transcription. Also, MHS subjects have higher Jph44 levels. At the same time, Figure 9 shows that the truncated Jph (mimicking Jph44) results in lower GSK3b expression. What was the protein and phosphorylation levels of this GSK3b? Also, would not a lower GSK3b correspond to less capacity to block GS and thus not be contributing to hyperglycemia as argued above? Please clarify.

10) Page 4, line 22-23 PhK reciprocally activates X… is followed by inhibits Y… Both describes a reduction/inhibition/antagonizing effect of PhK but by using an indirect and direct description, would be more reader friendly to use a direct description for both activities.

11) In the manuscript, the term "patients" are often used, but not specified if MHN or MHS, please clarify throughout the text.

12) Figure 2. Are these data from control mice? Or MHS-derived material?

13) Figure 3I, were these ca2+ measurements performed recently or associated to an earlier publication of the co-authors? Also, the 240 on the x-axis is cropped and x-axis is also partly cropped in 3J?

14) Figure 1 A and B show a western blot of proteins isolated from muscles of MHN and MHS individuals decorated with two different antibodies directed against JPH1. According to the manufacturer, antibody A is directed against the JPH1 protein sequence encompassing amino acids 387 to 512 while antibody B is directed against a no better specified C-terminal region of JPH1. Surprisingly, antibody B appears not to detect the full-length protein in lysates from human muscles, but recognizes only the 44 kDa fragment of JPH1. However, to the best of the reviewer's knowledge, antibody B has been reported by other laboratories to recognize the full-length JPH1 protein.

Thus, is not obvious why here this antibody should recognize only the shorter fragment. In addition, in MHS individuals there is no direct correlation between reduction in the content of the full-length JPH1 protein and appearance of the 44 kDa JPH1fragment, since, as also reported by the authors, no significant difference between MHN and MHS can be observed concerning the amount of the 44 kDa JPH1.

15) The authors show in supplemental Figure 1 that antibody B in total lysates from patients 164 and 167 preferentially recognizes the 44 kDa fragment of JPH1, but also a band at about 100 kDa.

Did the authors consider that the 100 kDa band may correspond to full-length JPH1, as also shown by Murphy et al., 2013 ?

Actually, according to Murphy et al., 2013, the 72 kDa protein detected by antibody A in this report represents a proteolytic fragment of full-length JPH1. Showing the entire membrane decorated with antibodies A and B may help to clarify these points.

Based on the data presented, it is very difficult to accept that antibody A and B have specific selectivity for JPH1 and the 44 kDa fragment of JPH1.

A good control would be to express the full length JPH1 and the JPH44 fragment and perform western blot and immunofluorescence staining with antibodies A and B. In the absence of direct evidence of the specificity of these staining, the Western Blots are not very convincing and the immunofluorescence data even more so.

16) In Figure 2B staining of a nucleus is shown only with antibody B against the 44 kDa JPH1 fragment, while no nucleus stained with antibody A is shown in Figure 2A. Images should all be at the same level of magnification and nuclear staining of nuclei with antibody A should be reported.

In Figure 2Db labeling of JPH1 covers both the nucleus and the cytoplasm, does it mean that JPH1 also goes to the nucleus? One would rather think that background immunofluorescence may provide a confounding staining and authors should be more cautious in interpreting these data.

Images in 2D and 2E refer to primary myotubes derived from patients. The authors show that RyR1 signals co-localizes with full-length JPH1, but not with the 44 kDa fragment, recognized by antibody B. How do the authors establish myotube differentiation?

Control (MHN) myotubes and myofibers should be shown as well. Can they provide images of entire myotubes, possibly captured at different Z planes? How can they exclude they are labeling perinuclear SR membranes? Can the authors show a Western blot analysis of proteins extracted from differentiated MHN and MHS myotubes showing immunoreactivity with the two antibodies?

17) Figure 3 A-C. The authors show images of a full-length JPH1 tagged with GFP at the N-terminus and FLAG at the C-terminus. In Figure 3Ad and Cd the Flag signal is all over the cytoplasm and the nuclei: since these are normal mouse cells and fibers, it is surprising that the FLAG signal is in the nuclei with an intensity of signal higher than in patient's muscle.

Can the authors supply images of entire myotubes, possibly captured in different Z planes? How can they distinguish between the cleaved and uncleaved JPH1 signals, especially in mouse myofibers, where calpain is supposed not to be so active as in MHS muscle fibers?

18) If the 44 kDa JPH1 fragment contains a transmembrane domain, it is difficult to understand the dual sarcoplasmic reticulum and nuclear localization. To justify this the authors, in the Discussion session, mention a hypothetical vesicular transport of the 44 kDa JPH1 fragment by vesicles. Traffic of proteins to the nucleus usually occurs through the nuclear pores and does not require vesicles. Even if diffusion from the SR membrane to the nuclear envelope occurs, the protein should remain in the compartment of the membrane envelope. There is no established evidence to support such an unusual movement inside the cells.

19) In Figure 5, the authors show the effect of Calpain1 on the full-length and 44 kDa JPH1 fragment in muscles from MHS patients. Can the authors repeat the same analysis on recombinant JPH1 tagged with GFP and FLAG? Can the authors provide images from MHN muscle fibers stained with JPH1 and Calpain1.

20) In Figure 6, the authors show images of MHS derived myotubes transfected with FLAG Calpain1 and compare the distribution of endogenous JPH1 and RYR1 in two cells, one expressing FLAG Calpain1 (cell1) and one not expressing the recombinant protein. They state that cell1 shows a strong signal of JPH1 in the nucleus, while this is not observed in cell2. Nevertheless, it is not clear where the nucleus is located within cell2 since the distribution of JPH1 is homogeneous across the cell. Can the authors show a different cell?

21) In Figure 7, panels Bb and Db: nuclei appear to stain positive for JPH1. It is not clear why in panels Ac, Bc they show a RYR1 staining while in panels Cc and Dc they show N-myc staining. The differential localization to nuclei appears rather poor also in these panels.

22) The strong nuclear staining in Figure 8, panels C and D is very different from the staining observed in Figure 2 and Figure 3. Transfection should not change the ratio between nuclear and cytoplasmic distribution.

23) Transcriptomic analysis was performed on a population of C2C12 transfected with the GFP-∆(1-240)JPH1 plasmid. Given that the muscles from MHS patients are available, the reviewer suggest performing transcriptomic analysis on muscle fibers from MHS patients as well.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The frequency of hyperglycemia is more than twofold greater in MHS patients than in the general age-matched population.
claims.source: Notably, and possibly as a consequence of reduced uptake and processing of glucose by muscle (Tammineni et al., 2020), the frequency of hyperglycemia (Altamirano et al., 2019) and diabetes (Tammineni et al., 2020) is more than twofold greater in MHS patients than in the general age-matched population.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The frequency of diabetes is more than twofold greater in MHS patients than in the general age-matched population.
claims.source: Notably, and possibly as a consequence of reduced uptake and processing of glucose by muscle (Tammineni et al., 2020), the frequency of hyperglycemia (Altamirano et al., 2019) and diabetes (Tammineni et al., 2020) is more than twofold greater in MHS patients than in the general age-matched population.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Hyperglycemia and diabetes in MHS patients is possibly a consequence of reduced uptake and processing of glucose by muscle.
claims.source: Notably, and possibly as a consequence of reduced uptake and processing of glucose by muscle (Tammineni et al., 2020), the frequency of hyperglycemia (Altamirano et al., 2019) and diabetes (Tammineni et al., 2020) is more than twofold greater in MHS patients than in the general age-matched population.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from previous work cited.

claims.claim: Graham Lamb and coworkers reported the cleavage of JPh1 and 2 in skeletal muscle and JPh2 in cardiac muscle in the presence of high cytosolic Ca2+ in 2013.
claims.source: In 2013, Graham Lamb and coworkers reported the cleavage of JPh1 and 2 in skeletal muscle and JPh2 in cardiac muscle in the presence of high [Ca2+]cyto, and associated it to the activation of calpain 1 (Murphy et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Cleavage of junctophilins in the presence of high cytosolic Ca2+ is associated with activation of calpain 1.
claims.source: In 2013, Graham Lamb and coworkers reported the cleavage of JPh1 and 2 in skeletal muscle and JPh2 in cardiac muscle in the presence of high [Ca2+]cyto, and associated it to the activation of calpain 1 (Murphy et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: JPh2 in cardiac muscle has a function similar to that of JPh1 in skeletal muscle — maintain structural integrity of the T-SR junction or dyad.
claims.source: In cardiac muscle, the junctophilin isoform JPh2 is known to have a function similar to that of JPh1 in skeletal muscle — maintain structural integrity of the T-SR junction or dyad (Takeshima et al., 2015; Lehnart and Wehrens, 2022; Perni, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Fragments of JPh2 have been shown to work in regulation of gene expression within nuclei.
claims.source: Strikingly, fragments of JPh2 have been shown to additionally work in regulation of gene expression within nuclei (Guo et al., 2018; Lahiri et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The content of full-size JPh1 is reduced in skeletal muscle of MHS patients.
claims.source: We now find that the content of full-size JPh1 is reduced in skeletal muscle of MHS patients, while a C-terminal, 44 kDa JPh1 fragment, which we refer to as JPh44, moves away from the triadic location of the full-size protein and relocates to the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A and C.

claims.claim: JPh44 moves away from the triadic location of the full-size protein and relocates to the nucleus.
claims.source: We now find that the content of full-size JPh1 is reduced in skeletal muscle of MHS patients, while a C-terminal, 44 kDa JPh1 fragment, which we refer to as JPh44, moves away from the triadic location of the full-size protein and relocates to the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B and Figure 3G-J.

claims.claim: The increased cleavage of JPh1 in MHS patients is due to activation of calpain1 by their higher cytosolic Ca2+.
claims.source: The observations indicate that the increased cleavage of JPh1 in MHS patients is due to activation of calpain1 by their higher [Ca2+]cyto.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing calpain1 activation (Figure 4), calcium-dependent cleavage (Figure 3D-F), and correlations (Figure 3I-J).

claims.claim: Proteolysis of JPh1 could contribute to de-stabilization of T-SR junctions.
claims.source: The proteolysis of JPh1, with possible de-stabilization of T-SR junctions (Komazaki et al., 2002; Ito et al., 2001), and the entry of its fragments into nuclei could contribute to the disease phenotype, as proposed for fragments of JPh2 produced in cardiac muscle of failing hearts (Guo et al., 2018; Lahiri et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from cited work on junctophilin function.

claims.claim: Entry of JPh1 fragments into nuclei could contribute to the disease phenotype.
claims.source: The proteolysis of JPh1, with possible de-stabilization of T-SR junctions (Komazaki et al., 2002; Ito et al., 2001), and the entry of its fragments into nuclei could contribute to the disease phenotype, as proposed for fragments of JPh2 produced in cardiac muscle of failing hearts (Guo et al., 2018; Lahiri et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from cited work on JPh2 fragments in cardiac muscle.

claims.claim: LS Song and colleagues provided evidence that the intra-nuclear actions of JPh2 fragments are 'stress-adaptive'.
claims.source: On the other hand, LS Song and colleagues (Guo et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022) provided evidence that the intra-nuclear actions of JPh2 fragments are 'stress-adaptive', partially offsetting the negative consequences of activation of proteolysis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: JPh2 fragments partially offset the negative consequences of activation of proteolysis.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: JPh44 contains segments capable of interaction with DNA.
claims.source: Given these precedents and the presence in the sequence of JPh44 of segments capable of interaction with DNA, here we tested the hypothesis that JPh44 exerts transcriptional control compensatory for the deleterious effects of elevated [Ca2+]cyto.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence analysis in Figure 4A showing helix-turn-helix DNA interaction site.

claims.claim: JPh44 exerts beneficial effects on the transcription and translation of enzymes active in glucose utilization by skeletal muscle.
claims.source: The study demonstrates beneficial effects of the fragment on the transcription and translation of enzymes active in glucose utilization by skeletal muscle.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing and protein expression data in Figure 8.

claims.claim: A large increase in cytosolic Ca2+ has been found in muscle fibers from MHS individuals.
claims.source: A large increase in [Ca2+]cyto has been found in muscle fibers from MHS individuals (Lopez et al., 1992), myotubes derived from MHS patient biopsies (Figueroa et al., 2019) and in MHS animal models (Lopez et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: MHS animals showed increased calpain activity.
claims.source: MHS animals also showed increased calpain activity (Michelucci et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Junctophilins are targets of Ca2+-activated calpain proteases.
claims.source: Given that junctophilins are targets of Ca2+-activated calpain proteases (Guo et al., 2018; Lahiri et al., 2020), we hypothesized that excess [Ca2+]cyto, by promotion of calpain activity, enhances JPh1 cleavage in MHS individuals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The 72 kDa band detected by antibody A corresponds to full JPh1 sequence or a form close to it.
claims.source: Because the 72–75 kDa migration weight is consistent with the full JPh1 sequence, we refer to this band as 'JPh1'. That the band is in some columns a doublet, and that it migrates slightly faster than the corresponding band in mouse muscle gels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicates that proteolytic degradation may take place in the human biopsies and this band may not correspond to the full sequence of JPh1.
claims.evidence: This is based on molecular weight analysis and comparison with mouse samples.

claims.claim: Antibody B specifically stains JPh44.
claims.source: A blot from a different gel, stained with anti-JPh1 antibody 'B' (raised against a more distal mouse JPh1 immunogen, 509–622) showed a greater content of a band with an effective migration size of ~44 kDa, referred to as JPh44 (Figure 1B and D, p=0.06). Blots in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrate that ab A reacts with both JPh1 and JPh44, while ab B fails to react with the 72 kDa protein, therefore constituting a useful tool for detection of JPh44 by immunofluorescence.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Antibody A reacts with both JPh1 and JPh44.
claims.source: Blots in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrate that ab A reacts with both JPh1 and JPh44, while ab B fails to react with the 72 kDa protein, therefore constituting a useful tool for detection of JPh44 by immunofluorescence.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The 72 kDa protein is overwhelmingly more abundant than its fragments, including JPh44.
claims.source: The 72 kDa protein is overwhelmingly more abundant than its fragments, including JPh44 in nearly every condition (as shown in Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and multiple documents later).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: There is a poor negative correlation between JPh1 reduction and JPh44 increase in individual subjects.
claims.source: While these results suggest that a greater cleavage of JPh1 leads to a reduction in its content, with consequent increase in the 44 kDa fragment, there is a poor negative correlation in individual subjects between the two changes (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis in Figure 1E showing R=-0.16.

claims.claim: The cleavage process may operate at multiple sites and sequentially on cleaved products, resulting in faster degradation of the full protein.
claims.source: A tentative explanation is that the cleavage process, which may operate at multiple sites and sequentially on cleaved products, results in faster degradation of the full protein, blurring any detailed correspondence between its disappearance and the increase in content of some fragments.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain the poor correlation observed.

claims.claim: Phosphorylase kinase (PhK) reciprocally activates glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthase.
claims.source: Phosphorylase kinase (PhK) reciprocally activates glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthase (GS).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about PhK function.

claims.claim: PhK is activated in the muscle of MHS patients.
claims.source: In previous work we demonstrated that this enzyme is activated in the muscle of MHS patients (Tammineni et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: PhK activation is consistent with an observed shift of the glycogen ←→glucose balance towards glycogenolysis.
claims.source: Its effects are consistent with an observed shift of the glycogen ←→glucose balance towards glycogenolysis (Tammineni et al., 2020), which is presumed responsible for the hyperglycemia and diabetes that develops in many of these patients (Tammineni et al., 2020; Altamirano et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from cited previous work.

claims.claim: The shift towards glycogenolysis is presumed responsible for the hyperglycemia and diabetes in MHS patients.

claims.evidence: This is based on inference from cited previous work.

claims.claim: GSK3β is a serine/threonine protein kinase that directly inhibits GS by phosphorylation.
claims.source: Here, we compared the contents of GSK3β, a serine/threonine protein kinase that directly inhibits GS by phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about GSK3β function.

claims.claim: The kinase activity of GSK3β is controlled by its phosphorylation at Ser 9.
claims.source: The kinase activity of GSK3β is controlled by its phosphorylation at Ser 9 and also promoted by truncation of the original ~47 kDa molecule to a form of ~40 kDa (Jin et al., 2015; Goñi-Oliver et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The kinase activity of GSK3β is promoted by truncation from ~47 kDa to ~40 kDa.
claims.source: The kinase activity of GSK3β is controlled by its phosphorylation at Ser 9 and also promoted by truncation of the original ~47 kDa molecule to a form of ~40 kDa (Jin et al., 2015; Goñi-Oliver et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The signal in the 47 kDa band of full-size GSK3β was reduced in MHS.
claims.source: The signal in the 47 kDa band of full-size GSK3β was reduced in MHS, while that of the activated 40 kDa fragment was increased.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1F-G.

claims.claim: The signal of the activated 40 kDa GSK3β fragment was increased in MHS.
claims.source: The signal in the 47 kDa band of full-size GSK3β was reduced in MHS, while that of the activated 40 kDa fragment was increased.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1F-H.

claims.claim: The changes in the two GSK3β forms were highly negatively correlated.
claims.source: The changes in the two proteins were highly negatively correlated (Figure 1I); consequently, the ratio of signals (40 kDa/47 kDa) was more than 3-fold greater in the MHS group, with high statistical significance.

claims.claim: The ratio of 40 kDa/47 kDa GSK3β signals was more than 3-fold greater in the MHS group.

claims.claim: There was a significant positive correlation between content of activated GSK3β form and serum glucose regardless of diagnosis.

claims.claim: The results are consistent with activation of the GS kinase by calpain proteolysis.
claims.source: These results are consistent with activation of the GS kinase by calpain proteolysis, which contributes to the shift in glycogen ←→glucose balance in favor of glycogenolysis, adding to the previously reported effect of inhibitory phosphorylation of GS (Tammineni et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the data and cited previous work.

claims.source: Hepatic and skeletal muscle silencing of the four genes named above improved the insulin resistance by inducing phosphorylation of Akt (Gómez-Valadés et al., 2008; Kern et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Lian et al., 2012; Hesselbarth et al., 2017).

claims.source: Therefore, the skeletal muscle fragment appears to have advantages over JPH2-NTP, to leave the junctional location (by losing most T-membrane anchors), and to reach inside nuclei, by having an additional NLS.

claims.source: The degree of autolysis of calpain in the samples that we analyzed is substantially greater than that reported for muscle tissue processed immediately after excision (Murphy et al., 2013; Murphy et al., 2006a; Murphy et al., 2007).

claims.source: An additional difference between the MHS condition and the stress of heart failure reported to unleash calpain cleavage of JPh2 is that the cardiac condition is accompanied by structural remodeling with loss of couplons and reduction in JPh2 content (Wu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2013), while no structural remodeling has been reported in muscle of MHS patients.

claims.evidence: This is based on absence of reports in the literature.

claims.claim: Studies of Ca2+ release function in MHS revealed an increase in muscle sensitivity to stimuli rather than major deficits expected from loss of functional junctions.
claims.source: Moreover, studies of Ca2+ release function revealed an increase in muscle sensitivity to stimuli (membrane voltage or calcium, e.g., Figueroa et al., 2019; Figueroa et al., 2021) rather than the major deficits expected to arise from a loss of functional junctions (Perni et al., 2017) upon JPh1 loss in the proportion observed here.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The presence of two junctophilin molecules (JPh1 and 2) that share a function provides a redundancy of paralogs.
claims.source: A speculative explanation recalls the expression of both JPh1 and 2 in skeletal muscle, both capable of sustaining calcium release function (Perni and Beam, 2022). The presence of two molecules that share a function — a redundancy of paralogs — would combine with a different level of redundancy, the presence of multiple copies of the same protein, perhaps polymerized (Rossi et al., 2019), to provide a 'sentinel' role.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on cited previous work.

claims.claim: Limited JPh1 cleavage would cause minimal or no deterioration of structure or function, while producing an adaptive gene-regulatory messenger.
claims.source: When proteolysis is activated in pathophysiological situations, limited JPh1 cleavage would cause minimal or no deterioration of structure or function, while producing an adaptive gene-regulatory messenger.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the functional consequences.

claims.claim: The elevated cytosolic Ca2+ in skeletal muscle of MHS individuals activates calpain1, which associates to T-SR junctions.
claims.source: We report that the elevated [Ca2+]cyto in skeletal muscle of individuals with MHS activates calpain1, which associates to T-SR junctions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective data presented.

claims.claim: The protease cleaves a kinase that inhibits glycogen synthase, an effect that correlates with and probably contributes to an increase in blood glucose concentration.
claims.source: The protease then cleaves a kinase that inhibits glycogen synthase, an effect that correlates with and probably contributes to an increase in blood glucose concentration.

claims.source: Cleavage of the kinase and that of GLUT4 promote the transition to hyperglycemia and diabetes found in many of these patients.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective data and previous work.

claims.claim: Calpain1 cleaves junctophilin1 to produce a C-terminal fragment of ~44 kDa that abandons junctions and enters nuclei.
claims.source: It also cleaves junctophilin1, to produce a C-terminal fragment of ~44 kDa that abandons junctions and enters nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective data presented.

claims.claim: In nuclei, the JPh44 fragment modulates transcription of multiple genes, resulting in effects opposing the deleterious alteration of the glucose utilization pathway.
claims.source: There, the fragment modulates transcription of multiple genes, resulting in effects opposing the deleterious alteration of the glucose utilization pathway.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the transcriptional data presented.

claims.claim: The JPh44 fragment is 'stress-adaptive'.
claims.source: Borrowing a term applied to a fragment of junctophilin2 found to enter nuclei in myocytes of failing hearts (Guo et al., 2018), the JPh44 fragment is therefore 'stress-adaptive'.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the beneficial transcriptional effects.

results.result: MHS patients show increased content of an activated 40 kDa GSK3β fragment with a more than 3-fold increase in the 40/47 kDa ratio, which correlates positively with serum glucose levels.
results.evaluation: Western blot data (Figure 1F-I) demonstrate statistically significant reciprocal changes in GSK3β forms between MHS and MHN patients, with strong negative correlation (R=-0.69, p<0.001) and significant correlation with serum glucose (Figure 1—supplement 3). The data are internally consistent and appropriately quantified.

results.result: MHS patients have reduced full-length JPh1 (~72 kDa) content with poor correlation to JPh44 fragment increase, suggesting complex proteolytic processing.
results.evaluation: Western blot data (Figure 1A, C) show statistically significant ~50% reduction in JPh1 in MHS patients (p<0.001). The poor correlation (R=-0.16) between JPh1 loss and JPh44 gain is acknowledged and reasonably explained by multi-site sequential cleavage. Antibody specificity is validated (Figure 1—supplement 2).

results.result: JPh44 relocates from T-SR junctions to nuclei, while full-length JPh1 remains highly colocalized with RyR1 at junctions.
results.evaluation: High-resolution immunofluorescence with multiple colocalization metrics (R, ICQ, Van Steensel shift, FWHM in Table 1) demonstrates clear spatial separation. JPh1 shows high colocalization with RyR1 (R=0.88, VS shift=21 nm) while JPh44 does not (R=0.31, VS shift=66 nm). All four metrics show statistically significant differences (p<0.001). The methodology is rigorous.

results.result: Doubly-tagged JPh1 (GFP-JPh1-FLAG) demonstrates that JPh44 is a C-terminal fragment, with the N-terminus remaining at junctions and C-terminus entering nuclei.
results.evaluation: The differential distribution of N-terminal GFP (cytosolic/nuclear ratio ~3-1000 fold higher than FLAG) across multiple cell types (Table 2) provides strong evidence for C-terminal cleavage. The approach is elegant and the quantification is statistically significant across biological replicates.

results.result: Elevated cytosolic Ca2+ drives JPh1 cleavage and nuclear JPh44 accumulation in MHS patients.
results.evaluation: Multiple lines of evidence converge: (1) Ca2+-dependent cleavage in permeabilized fibers (Figure 3D-F), (2) increased nuclear JPh44 in MHS patients (Figure 3G-H, p<0.001), (3) positive correlations between nuclear JPh44 and cytosolic Ca2+ (R=0.48, p=0.04 and R=0.88, p=0.004 in Figure 3I-J). The correlations are statistically significant with appropriate sample sizes.

results.result: Computational prediction identifies the most likely calpain1 cleavage site at R240-S241 (or S233-S234), which would generate a ~44-46 kDa C-terminal fragment containing nuclear localization sequences.
results.evaluation: GPS-CCD 1.0 prediction (Figure 4B) identifies conserved cleavage sites across mammalian orthologs with consistent molecular weight predictions (45.92-46.28 kDa, Figure 4D). The predicted fragment contains two NLS sequences (Figure 4A). The computational approach is appropriate and predictions are consistent with experimental observations.

results.result: Calpain1 is activated in MHS patients (74% higher 76/80 kDa ratio, p=0.029) and correlates negatively with JPh1 and GSK3β content and positively with activated GSK3β fragment.
results.evaluation: Western blot analysis (Figure 4E-J) shows calpain1 autolysis with statistically significant ratio differences and strong correlations (R=-0.65 for JPh1, R=-0.64 for GSK3β, R=0.61 for 40 kDa GSK3β, all p≤0.001). The custom quantification method is validated. The correlations provide strong mechanistic support.

results.result: Calpain1 directly cleaves JPh1 in vitro in a time- and dose-dependent manner, is inhibited by MDL 28170, and colocalizes with JPh1 but not JPh44 at T-SR junctions.
results.evaluation: In vitro cleavage experiments (Figure 5A-F) demonstrate reciprocal changes in JPh1/JPh44 completed in 5 min, dose-dependent effects, and inhibition by calpain inhibitor. Immunofluorescence (Figure 5G-H, Table 3) shows calpain1 colocalization with JPh1 but not JPh44. Multiple independent lines of evidence support the mechanism.

results.result: Overexpression of FLAG-calpain1 in myotubes increases nuclear JPh localization and reduces JPh-RyR1 colocalization, with calpain1 localizing to T-SR junctions.
results.evaluation: Transfection experiments (Figure 6, Tables 4-6) show large, highly significant increase in nuclear JPh (Table 4, p<0.001) and reduced JPh-RyR1 colocalization (Table 5, all 4 metrics p≤0.023) in calpain-expressing cells. Calpain1 colocalizes with RyR1 at junctions (Table 6). The within-field comparison controls for experimental variation.

results.result: GFP-Δ(1-240) JPh1 deletion mutant mimics native JPh44 behavior, moving away from triads into the I band and accumulating in nuclei.
results.evaluation: Immunofluorescence in mouse FDB fibers (Figure 7, Table 7) shows the deletion construct behaves similarly to native JPh44: reduced colocalization with RyR1 (statistically significant differences in R, VS shift, FWHM) and nuclear localization. This validates the predicted cleavage site and provides a functional surrogate for JPh44.

results.result: Expression of GFP-Δ(1-240) JPh1 in myoblasts alters transcription of 160 genes (p<0.01), including reduced expression of GSK3β and multiple inhibitors of the PI3K-Akt-glucose pathway.
results.evaluation: RNA sequencing (Figure 8B-C) identifies 121 repressed and 39 induced genes with KEGG pathway enrichment analysis showing involvement in glucose metabolism. Key findings are validated by qRT-PCR (Figure 8D) showing ~50% reduction in GSK3β, TRAF3, NGFR, and Repin1 mRNA. The transcriptional approach is appropriate for identifying potential JPh44 functions.

results.result: Expression of GFP-Δ(1-240) JPh1 reduces GSK3β protein levels by 40% in transfected cells compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Western blot analysis (Figure 8E-F) and high-resolution imaging (Figure 8H, Table 8) both demonstrate statistically significant reduction in GSK3β protein in cells expressing the deletion construct. The dual approach (population-level WB and single-cell imaging) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Elevated cytosolic Ca2+ in MHS activates calpain1, which cleaves both JPh1 and GSK3β, with the latter contributing to impaired glycogen synthesis and hyperglycemia.
results.evaluation: This integrative result is supported by: (1) Ca2+-dependent calpain activation (Figure 4), (2) calpain-mediated cleavage of both substrates (Figures 1, 5), (3) correlations between calpain activation and substrate cleavage (Figure 4H-J), (4) correlation between activated GSK3β and serum glucose (Figure 1—supplement 3). The multi-step pathway is well-documented.

results.result: JPh44 functions as a stress-adaptive transcriptional regulator that opposes glucose dysregulation by reducing expression of GSK3β and inhibitors of glucose utilization.
results.evaluation: While the transcriptional data (Figure 8) show that the JPh44 surrogate reduces expression of genes that would improve glucose utilization, this is demonstrated only in myoblasts with an artificial construct. Direct evidence that endogenous JPh44 has these effects in MHS patients is lacking. The functional consequences of the transcriptional changes on actual glucose metabolism are not demonstrated. This remains a well-supported hypothesis requiring validation.

results.result: GSK3β is a serine/threonine kinase that inhibits glycogen synthase through phosphorylation, with activity controlled by Ser9 phosphorylation and promoted by truncation to 40 kDa.
results.evaluation: These are well-established facts about GSK3β function supported by appropriate citations (Jin et al., 2015; Goñi-Oliver et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2012). The claims represent accepted knowledge in the field.

results.result: Junctophilin (isoforms 1 and 2) is one of five essential proteins for EC coupling, functioning as a structural protein that maintains T-SR junctions in striated muscle.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge about junctophilin function, supported by appropriate citations (Takeshima et al., 2000; Komazaki et al., 2002; Rossi et al., 2019; Perni et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018). This provides necessary background context.

results.result: MHS is characterized by RyR1 gain-of-function mutations leading to increased channel leak, SR Ca2+ depletion, and elevated resting cytosolic Ca2+ (485 nM in MHS vs 112 nM in MHN).
results.evaluation: These claims describe the established pathophysiology of MHS, supported by appropriate citations including the key Lopez et al., 1992 study reporting the Ca2+ concentrations. This provides essential background for understanding the current work.

results.result: MHS patients have more than twofold higher frequency of hyperglycemia and diabetes compared to age-matched controls, likely due to impaired muscle glucose processing.
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by citations to previous work (Altamirano et al., 2019; Tammineni et al., 2020; DeFronzo and Tripathy, 2009). The epidemiological observation and mechanistic hypothesis provide important motivation for the current study.

results.result: Calpain1 cleaves junctophilins in response to elevated Ca2+ (50-300 nM range), with activation involving autolysis from 80 kDa to 76 kDa.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge about calpain1 function, supported by appropriate citations (Murphy et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2018; Lahiri et al., 2020; Goll et al., 2003). This provides necessary mechanistic background.

results.result: In cardiac muscle, JPh2 is cleaved by calpains producing fragments that enter nuclei and regulate gene expression, with N-terminal fragments being stress-adaptive and C-terminal fragments causing hypertrophy.
results.evaluation: These claims describe previous work on cardiac JPh2, supported by appropriate citations (Guo et al., 2018; Lahiri et al., 2020; Takeshima et al., 2015). This provides important precedent for the nuclear functions of junctophilin fragments discovered in the current study.

results.result: Previous work demonstrated PhK activation and GLUT4 translocation defects in MHS patients, contributing to a shift toward glycogenolysis.
results.evaluation: These claims summarize previous findings from Tammineni et al., 2020, providing context for how the current GSK3β and JPh44 findings fit into a broader understanding of glucose dysregulation in MHS.

results.result: Calpain1 binds to cellular structures immediately upon Ca2+ elevation, restricting its proteolytic activity to nearby substrates, consistent with its junctional localization.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic detail is supported by citations (Murphy et al., 2006b; Murphy, 2009) and is consistent with the colocalization data showing calpain1 at junctions (Tables 3, 6). This explains the spatial specificity of JPh1 cleavage.

results.result: The link between GSK3β activity and diabetes in skeletal muscle is well-established, and this study provides the first demonstration of GSK3β regulation by proteolysis in skeletal muscle.
results.evaluation: The established link is supported by appropriate citations (Henriksen and Dokken, 2006). The novelty claim about proteolytic regulation in skeletal muscle (vs. brain) is supported by the data and citation to Jin et al., 2015 for the brain findings. The correlation with fasting blood sugar (Figure 1—supplement 3) validates the physiological relevance.

results.result: Previous studies show that silencing TRAF3, Repin1, Pck1, Ces3a, Rbp4, Apoc3, MEG3, and NGFR improves insulin resistance through various mechanisms.
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by appropriate citations describing the roles of these genes in glucose metabolism. This provides important context for interpreting the transcriptional changes induced by the JPh44 surrogate.

results.result: Proteolysis of JPh1 could contribute to T-SR junction destabilization and the disease phenotype, and nuclear localization of JPh44 suggests a role in gene transcription.
results.evaluation: These are speculative claims based on analogy to cardiac JPh2 and the observed nuclear localization. While reasonable hypotheses, they are not directly tested. The study does not demonstrate junction destabilization in MHS patients, and the transcriptional role is inferred rather than proven for endogenous JPh44.

results.result: The poor correlation between JPh1 loss and JPh44 gain may result from multi-site sequential cleavage, and perinuclear FLAG accumulation in mouse myofibers may reflect steep concentration gradients or nuclear membrane barriers.
results.evaluation: These are speculative explanations for observed phenomena. While plausible, they are not directly tested. The explanations are reasonable but remain hypotheses that would require additional experiments to validate.

results.result: MDL 28170 inhibition is consistent with calpain1-specific cleavage but doesn't exclude calpain2 or cathepsin B; calpain1 activation likely explains decreased GLUT4 translocation through proteolysis.
results.evaluation: The limitation regarding inhibitor specificity is appropriately acknowledged. The connection to GLUT4 is inferred from cited work (Otani et al., 2004) but not directly demonstrated in this study. These are reasonable inferences but not proven.

results.result: Unlike JPH2-NTP, JPh44 loses N-terminal MORN motifs but retains a second NLS, potentially providing advantages for leaving junctions and entering nuclei.
results.evaluation: This structural comparison is based on sequence analysis and speculation about functional consequences. While the sequence differences are clear, the proposed functional advantages are speculative and not directly tested. The reasoning is plausible but requires experimental validation.

results.result: The degree of calpain autolysis in analyzed samples is greater than in freshly processed tissue, indicating some post-excision protein degradation, introducing uncertainty about fragment sequences but not precluding MHS vs MHN comparisons.
results.evaluation: This is an appropriately acknowledged limitation. The comparison with published data (Murphy et al., 2013) is valid, and the reasoning that uniform treatment allows valid comparisons between groups is sound. This represents good scientific practice in acknowledging limitations.

results.result: Unlike heart failure, MHS shows no structural remodeling despite JPh1 reduction, possibly due to redundancy from JPh1/JPh2 paralogs and multiple protein copies, allowing limited cleavage to produce adaptive signals without functional deterioration.
results.evaluation: The absence of reported structural remodeling in MHS is noted, and the functional studies (Figueroa et al., 2019, 2021) showing increased sensitivity rather than deficits are cited. However, the proposed redundancy mechanism is speculative. This is a reasonable hypothesis to explain an apparent paradox but lacks direct experimental support.

results.result: Previous work by LS Song's group showed JPH2-NTP fragments have stress-adaptive effects, and calpain expression appears to improve RyR1 expression and clustering.
results.evaluation: The JPH2-NTP findings are supported by appropriate citations (Guo et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022). The observation about RyR1 in calpain-expressing cells (Figure 6) is noted but acknowledged as not pursued further, with citation to developmental roles (Goll et al., 1992). This is appropriately presented as an observation rather than a main finding.
